title: The Work, and the Job
segs: Chapter 47. The Work, and the Job.

Rhea Kapoor telephoned on a Sunday evening in June. She began, as people do who have rehearsed an apology, with the end of it. She knew this was Anaya's only free night, she said, and she wouldn't keep her long.

Anaya had met Rhea in the autumn at a meetup, where Rhea had asked the one question nobody else wanted to ask the speaker. Rhea had spent six years delivering technology programmes for government departments, with a steering committee every month and a status report every Friday. Since then she had spent a year working through every part of what Anaya had spent a year doing, alone and at night.

And she had built something of her own: a small tool that read a week of customer-support tickets, sorted them into themes, and wrote the report a support lead used to spend a day on. Ten design partners had used it. But she had shown the work to nobody who could give her a job.

Rhea had ten job advertisements open, and all of them said "AI product manager". She couldn't see why she would be right for any of them. Anaya asked her to send the ten, and to say what her resume said at the top. After a pause Rhea said that it said she was passionate about AI.
The case: ten advertisements and one resume.

The sections that follow are the work of a few Sunday evenings. They come last in the book because they use everything before them. They also teach the skill that most people leave out: showing what you have done.
One title, six jobs.

The first thing to understand, Anaya told Rhea, is that the title is a label stuck onto at least six different jobs. The table shows them, and what each kind of employer wants from the person it hires.

Table 47.1: Six jobs behind one title. Adds AI features to an existing product. What it builds: Features for users it already has. What it wants: Judgement, a record of shipping, and the ability to work with people who build models. Builds something that would not exist without AI. What it builds: A new product. What it wants: Speed, prototyping, comfort with a thing that sometimes fails, and a habit of measuring. Makes tools, interfaces and models for other teams. What it builds: Platforms. What it wants: Technical depth and an understanding of what a developer finds painful. Builds AI for its own employees. What it builds: Internal tools. What it wants: Someone who can make people change how they work, keep it secure, and show hours saved. A consulting firm that builds AI systems for clients. What it builds: Projects for other organisations, often large ones. What it wants: Delivery discipline, plain writing, evaluation and governance, and the nerve to tell a client what a system cannot do. A public-sector or digital-public-infrastructure body. What it builds: Services for citizens, often in several languages and sometimes by voice. What it wants: Field deployments, Indic languages and voice, ministry stakeholders, and open-weight options.

The six ask for different evidence, Anaya said, so one resume can't serve all ten advertisements. For someone who has delivered technology projects, three are open doors: a company built on AI, a consulting firm that builds AI systems for clients, and a public-sector body.

Rhea's six years sat closest to the third. Then she asked Rhea to do something dull. Put the ten advertisements across the top of a sheet. Down the left side, write every skill any of them mentions. Tick the box wherever a role asks for a skill.

When the sheet is finished, the rows with the most ticks show what the market wants. The rows with none are noise. This sheet is a role matrix. For each row, Rhea was to make one more mark, and to make it honestly: for her, was the skill proven, partly proven or missing?

It took Rhea three evenings. She sent the sheet back with a note: she had done most of what they wanted, and she hadn't said it in a way anyone could check. Anaya told her to say it in terms of what she had proved. "I shipped an AI product to ten real users and raised its useful-result rate from fifty-eight percent to seventy-one" is a sentence, she said. "Passionate about AI" is a mood.
What goes on the page.
They rewrote the resume over two Sundays, and the method was one sentence long. Every line should say what she did, what she decided and what happened. The table shows two lines before and after.

Table 47.2: Resume lines before and after. Worked on an AI tool for support teams. After: Built a theme-finding tool for support tickets; chose to ground every theme in quoted phrases, and raised the share of themes marked useful from 58% to 71% across ten partner teams. Responsible for testing. After: Wrote a fixed test set of twenty past weeks and used it to stop two releases that would have lowered accuracy.
The second line, Anaya pointed out, tells the reader that Rhea thinks about quality before she ships. The reader doesn't need her to say it.
Next came the case study: a one- or two-page account of one piece of work. Rhea's would answer six questions, in order.

What was the problem, and what evidence showed it was real? What did you decide, and what did you reject? What did you give up, knowingly? What happened, in numbers? What went wrong, and what did you change? What would you do next?
The fifth question does the work, Anaya said. Anybody can describe a success, and people hire someone who knows what broke. She advised two case studies, not six.

They should sit where a recruiter will find them: a small page of Rhea's own, linked from the top of her profile. The headline of the profile should name the job Rhea wanted and one thing she had proved. It should say nothing about being a lifelong learner.
The four questions that every loop asks.
In the middle of June they began on the interviews. Anaya started by describing how most interview loops are built. There are four kinds of question, and each has a shape you can follow.

Table 47.3: Four kinds of interview question. Product sense. An example: Design a voice assistant for a state helpline, in two languages. A shape to follow: Clarify the goal, pick a user, list their problems, choose one, propose solutions, rank them, say how you would measure it. Strategy. An example: Should we enter the Indian market? A shape to follow: Goal, market, customer, competitors, our advantage, then a recommendation and its risks. Metrics. An example: Daily users fell ten percent. Why? A shape to follow: Check the data is right, internal or external cause, which segment, which step, hypotheses, how to test them. Execution. An example: Two teams want the same engineer. What do you do? A shape to follow: What each is worth, the options, the trade-offs, a decision, how you tell people.

Product sense is the ability to choose a user, find their real problem and propose a sensible solution. It frightened people most, because it seemed to need an inspiration they didn't have. It doesn't. It needs the habit of choosing a user before proposing anything, and after a year of work, Rhea's habit was good.

She practised on a prompt from a world she knew: a voice assistant for a state helpline, in two languages. Her first three moves were short. She clarified the goal, which was fewer callers waiting and fewer wrong answers about a scheme's rules, not a clever assistant.

She chose one user, a caller on a basic phone who speaks only the regional language and rings at the end of a working day. And she listed that caller's problems before naming any feature: not knowing which scheme applies, not knowing which papers to bring, and being cut off when the line is bad. Only then did she say which of the three she would solve first.

Anaya's advice was to say the structure aloud before starting: something like "I'll clarify, pick a user, find the problems and then choose". That way the interviewer can follow. If they want the candidate somewhere else, they can say so in the first minute and not the fortieth.
And at the end, choose. Interviewers want to watch a candidate commit to a decision and give reasons. People who list five options and recommend none fail at this more than at anything else.

She rehearsed a metrics question that night. Daily users had fallen ten percent. Rhea began by asking whether the number itself could be wrong: a change to how it was counted, or a broken event. That is the first correct move, Anaya said, and most candidates skip it.
Designing a system out loud.

The question most particular to the new kind of job, and the one Rhea feared, was the design interview. An interviewer says: design a support assistant for our product. This is the system-design interview, and it asks for no code. It asks for a sign that the candidate can think about an AI feature as a whole.
Anaya gave her six steps, and Rhea wrote them in the order she would say them.

Table 47.4: Six steps for a system-design answer. 1. Users and task. What to say: Who it is for, the task, and what success looks like. 2. Approach. What to say: A model alone, or a model with documents to find answers in, or a fixed workflow, or an agent, and why. 3. Evaluation. What to say: How you would know it worked before launch and after. 4. Failure. What to say: What happens when it is wrong, slow or attacked. 5. Cost and delay. What to say: A rough cost for one task, and the delay users will tolerate. 6. Rollout. What to say: To whom first, what you would measure, and when you would turn it back.

Use numbers, she told Rhea, even rough ones. For example: about two thousand words of context in and three hundred out for each question, so under a rupee. Numbers show that the candidate knows the thing costs money each time it runs. Anaya had once watched a very good candidate lose a job by never mentioning cost.
Rhea said slowly that everything in the year had been preparation for this. Anaya said it was the same year.
Telling stories about yourself.
The last kind of question is the oldest: tell me about a time you disagreed with an engineer. The interviewer asks about the candidate's past because it is the best guide to the future they have.

Anaya told Rhea to prepare six to eight true stories from real work, and to tell each one in the same four parts. People call this the STAR method: the situation, the task, the action and the result. Most of the time goes to what the candidate did, not to what the team did, because the interviewer is interviewing the candidate.
They worked on one story for an hour. It was about a decision that had gone wrong, because those make the best stories.
Worked example: Rhea's story in four parts.

Situation: the first version of my tool let an agent choose the steps for the weekly report. Task: I owned making it reliable enough for ten design partners. Action: I expected the agent to cope better with unusual weeks, so I kept it. When three of my twenty test weeks failed, I built the same flow as a fixed workflow and ran both on the same weeks. Result: the workflow failed once in twenty and was twice as fast, so I switched. I learned to measure both options before committing, and I do that now for every large design choice.
It is a good story, Anaya said, because the wrong decision was real, and the repair came from measuring, not from apologising.
The question about her title.

In the second round the interviewer put down the script and picked up the resume. Six years of programme delivery for government departments, he said, sounds like programme management. Why should he believe she could own a product?

Anaya had expected it, and they had rehearsed it on a Sunday. The answer was not to argue with the label. It was to name three decisions Rhea had owned. The first was what she refused to build: her tool could have answered questions about the report in a chat box, and she left that out because she could not measure it.

The second was the threshold that stopped a release: her fixed test set had held back two versions. The third was the number she was accountable for, the share of themes marked useful, which went from 58 to 71 percent.

Then Rhea turned the history into an asset. Six years in a regulated sector meant audits, data-location rules and sign-offs from people who could say no. Most candidates would have to claim that from a reading list. She did not say she had been a product manager. She said she had owned an outcome, and she could show the number.
Building while they watch.
Some loops add a round in which the candidate builds something small, live, with a coding assistant, while the interviewer watches. It tests judgement more than typing.

Anaya's advice came from the verifier idea earlier in the book: before asking the assistant for anything, say how you will check its work. State the check aloud, such as "the result must hide every number in my ten sample messages". Ask for small steps.

Read what comes back, and say what you would not trust yet. Interviewers watch whether the candidate can tell a change that worked from one that only looks right. A half-finished build whose checks pass is a better result than a finished one that nobody has checked.
Alone, and with other people.

Two small matters remained. The first is the take-home: a task set by an employer to be done alone, in a stated time. Keep to the time. Put your assumptions at the top, and end with what you would do with more time. Reviewers prefer a clear, honest answer to a long one. A person who says what they left out is trusted more than one who pretends there was nothing.

The second is networking, which Rhea disliked. It worked best when she had something to show. Anaya's advice was not to ask people for a referral. Instead, send a specific person the case study and ask one specific question about it, because that is a question they can answer.

Pay was a matter of preparation. Learn what the role usually pays in that city. Let the company make the first offer. Then ask once, politely, with a reason, such as another offer or the size of the job.
What happened.

It would be pleasant to report that Rhea was hired within the month. She wasn't. Two of the ten companies asked her back for a second round, after the resume and case study had been rewritten as agreed.

By the third week of July she was in a room with a woman who asked her to design a support assistant for the company's product. Rhea said aloud, a little shakily, "I'll start with who uses it and what a good outcome is."

Anaya wasn't there. She heard about it afterwards, in a telephone call in which Rhea described the question and said that halfway through she had realised she was no longer rehearsing. She was explaining something she had made.
Key idea: What you can now say.
Fill each N from your own project.

My case study names what broke, N things, and the number that moved, from N to N. I priced it by who pays: one message costs N rupees to serve, and the margin stays above N percent at ten times the base use. I count what people do without keeping what they wrote: N measures, and none of them stores a message.
Chapter summary.

"AI product manager" names at least six different jobs. So the useful first step is to put real job advertisements into a role matrix, mark each skill as proven, partly proven or missing, and position yourself on what you can prove.

Each line of a resume says what was done, what was decided and what resulted. A case study adds the options rejected, the trade-offs, the numbers, what failed and what comes next. Interview loops ask four kinds of question: product sense, strategy, metrics and execution. Each is answered by naming a structure aloud and then committing to a choice. The system-design interview wants approach, evaluation, failure, cost and rollout, spoken with rough numbers. A resume that reads like programme management is answered with three decisions you owned and a number, not by arguing about the label. In a live build round, state the check before you ask the assistant for the work. Stories about your past are told in four parts, with most of the time on your own action. A take-home states its assumptions and what it leaves out. Networking starts with a specific question and a piece of work. A negotiation begins with research, and asks once.
